title: What Is Ojang? How to Read Korea's Five-Day Market Dates
desc: Korea's traditional five-day markets don't run on weekdays — they run on a five-day date cycle. Here's how to read "days ending in 2 and 7" and actually show up on the right day.
body:
If you've read anything about Korea's traditional markets, you've probably seen a line like "open on days ending in 2 and 7" and wondered what it actually means. It isn't a weekday. It's a five-day cycle tied to the calendar date, and once you know the rule it takes about five seconds to decode any market's schedule in the country.

The rule: it's about the last digit of the date

Korea's traditional five-day markets — called ojang (오일장) — open every five days, based on the last digit of the day of the month. A market described as a "2 and 7" market opens on the 2nd, 7th, 12th, 17th, 22nd, and 27th of every month. A "5 and 10" market opens on the 5th, 10th, 15th, 20th, 25th, and 30th. There are five possible combinations in total: 1 & 6, 2 & 7, 3 & 8, 4 & 9, and 5 & 10. It has nothing to do with the day of the week, so a market day can fall on a Tuesday one week and a Sunday the next.

Reference table

Market typeOpens on (each month)
1 & 6-day market1, 6, 11, 16, 21, 26
2 & 7-day market2, 7, 12, 17, 22, 27
3 & 8-day market3, 8, 13, 18, 23, 28
4 & 9-day market4, 9, 14, 19, 24, 29
5 & 10-day market5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30

Nearby markets deliberately avoid sharing a schedule. Historically, itinerant traders (bobusang) walked a five-village circuit, spending one day in each village before the cycle repeated — so neighboring towns picked different end-digits, and merchants and buyers weren't split between two markets on the same day. That's why two markets a short drive apart often have market days one day apart, which makes it easy to combine two into a single trip.

Real examples from official English listings

Here's what that looks like in practice, quoting the official day descriptions exactly as published by the Korea Tourism Organization:

  • Eonyang Alps Market Town (Ulsan) — "On the 2nd, 7th, 12th, 17th, 22nd, and 27th of each month"
  • Guryongpo Fifth-Day Market (Pohang) — "Every 3rd, 8th, 13th, 18th, 23rd, 28th"
  • Hallim Traditional 5-Day Market (Jeju) — opens on dates ending in 4 and 9
  • Yongmun Millennium Market (Gyeonggi) — "Days ending in 5 and 10," right in front of Yongmun Station

You can browse all of these — plus Korea's larger, permanent traditional markets — on Chukjemoa's Markets page, where each five-day market shows a countdown to its next open day.

What time to go

Markets change character through the day. Vendors set up between 7 and 9am, and that's when perishables like vegetables, wild greens, and seafood are freshest. Late morning to noon is the busiest and fullest stretch. By mid-afternoon, popular items are often already gone — but vendors sometimes drop prices sharply in the last hour or two before closing, so if you're bargain-hunting rather than shopping for something specific, a late-afternoon visit can work in your favor.

Before you go

  • Bring cash. Larger stalls increasingly take cards, but small vendors are still mostly cash-only.
  • Public holidays can cancel a market day. Markets often don't open on Lunar New Year or Chuseok itself, and severe weather can cancel a market day too — when in doubt, a quick call to the local market office confirms it.
  • Bring a foldable bag or cart if you're planning to buy produce — most stalls don't hand out bags automatically.

Planning to combine a market visit with a festival on the same trip? Use Festival Finder to see what's happening in the same region on your dates.

title: What to Buy at a Korean Five-Day Market — And What's Actually There
desc: The Korea Tourism Organization's English-language market data covers 34 traditional markets. Here's an honest breakdown of what's for sale, and which ones are genuine five-day markets vs. permanent daily markets.
body:
"Go check out a five-day market" is easy advice to give and confusing to act on, because most sources tell you when a market opens but not what it actually sells. Some are packed with produce and wild greens; others are almost entirely clothing and household goods. Show up expecting one and finding the other, and the trip can feel like a waste.

First, a distinction the name doesn't make obvious

Chukjemoa's English market page currently lists 34 markets sourced from official Korea Tourism Organization data. But only 6 of those 34 are true five-day (ojang) markets that follow the date-cycle rule described in our guide to reading market days. The other 28 — including well-known names like Jagalchi Fish Market in Busan, Gwangjang and Dongdaemun in Seoul, and Gukje Market in Busan — are permanent markets open every day of the week. Both types are worth knowing about, but they're different experiences: the five-day markets are smaller, local, and only worth timing a trip around; the permanent markets are open whenever you happen to show up.

What's actually for sale

Looking at the official sale-item descriptions across all 34 listings, the most commonly mentioned categories are:

  • Clothing — mentioned at 9 markets
  • Fish / seafood — mentioned at 15 markets combined (fresh and dried)
  • General goods — 5 markets
  • Fruit — 5 markets
  • Vegetables — 4 markets
  • Agricultural produce — 4 markets
  • Meat — 3 markets

A few markets specialize hard enough to be worth a trip on their own. Seoul Gyeongdong Market is built around Oriental medicine ingredients and dried seafood. Jagalchi Market in Busan is almost entirely fresh and dried fish. Hwanghak-dong Flea Market (also called the "Dokkaebi Market") deals in antiques, old furniture, cameras, and watches rather than food at all. If there's one specific thing you want to buy, checking a market's listed specialty first will save a trip to the wrong place.

Practical notes the data can confirm

Parking information is listed for 29 of the 34 markets, and most describe some form of available parking — though exact capacity is rarely given, so arriving early on a market day is still the safer bet. Opening hours are inconsistent across listings: some markets state fixed hours (Jungmun 5-day Market on Jeju, for example, runs 9am–5pm), while others simply note that hours vary by store, which is common for markets built from many independently-run stalls.

For the six real five-day markets, the smart move is checking the actual market day before you go — Chukjemoa's Markets page shows each one's schedule and, where the official market-day text is available, a live countdown to the next opening.

title: Korean Public Holidays and Why They Change Your Festival Plans
desc: Korea's two biggest holidays, Lunar New Year and Chuseok, reshape which festivals are actually running on any given day. Here's how the 2026 Chuseok holiday breaks down, and what that means for travel timing.
body:
If you're building a Korea trip around a major national holiday, it's worth knowing that festivals don't run at a constant rate through the holiday period. Small, single-day community events mostly pause on the holiday itself, while large, weeks-long events — flower festivals, expos, light festivals — keep running regardless. Which kind of festival you're chasing changes which day of the holiday is actually worth traveling on.

Chuseok 2026, for reference

Chuseok (Korean Thanksgiving) falls on Friday, September 25, 2026. The public holiday runs from Thursday, September 24 through Saturday, September 26, and with Sunday the 27th immediately following, it functions as a four-day break for most people. (If the 26th's overlap with a Saturday triggers a substitute holiday, that would add Monday the 28th — check official government sources closer to the date for final confirmation.)

The pattern: festivals build through the holiday, not evenly

Using Korea Tourism Organization data on 922 festival and event listings, here's how many were running on each day of the 2026 Chuseok period (based on typical prior-year scheduling for recurring events — individual festivals can move their dates year to year, so treat this as a pattern rather than a 2026 guarantee):

DateFestivals running
Sept 24 (Thu, holiday start)62
Sept 25 (Fri, Chuseok day)68
Sept 26 (Sat)89
Sept 27 (Sun, holiday end)109

That's a 1.76x difference between the first and last day of the same four-day holiday. The reason is straightforward: local governments and neighborhood associations generally don't hold community events on the holiday's core days, when people are traveling to see family and observing ancestral rites. Once those obligations are done, smaller local festivals cluster into the back half of the break.

What keeps running on the holiday itself

The festivals that do run through the entire period tend to be longer-format events rather than single-day community festivals — expos, flower festivals timed to a bloom season, and night-lighting events that already span several weeks regardless of the holiday. If your trip window is fixed around the earlier days of a Korean holiday, a long-running event is a much safer bet than a single-day local festival.

What this means for planning

  • Arriving early in a holiday period? Prioritize multi-week events over single-day local festivals — check Festival Finder filtered by your travel dates to see what's actually confirmed running.
  • Traditional markets follow their own date rule independent of the holiday calendar — see our guide to Korea's market days — but many also skip the holiday's core day or two, so a direct check is worth it if a market visit is central to your plan.
  • Use When to Go to see a month-by-month view of what's typically running before locking in dates.

As with any recurring event, individual festival dates are set by local organizers and can shift year to year — always confirm directly with the festival's official channel before finalizing travel.

title: Why You Can't Find a Place to Eat Near a Korean Festival
desc: We cross-referenced 922 Korean festivals against 6,620 registered restaurants by location. The results explain why "just walk out and find something" works in Seoul and fails almost everywhere else.
body:
One of the most common regrets after visiting a Korean festival isn't about the festival itself — it's "we never actually got a proper meal." Food stalls inside the festival grounds have long lines and high prices; stepping outside the venue means gambling on the unknown; and the restaurant you found online turns out to be closed for a break, or closed for the day entirely.

To find out whether this is bad luck or a structural pattern, we cross-referenced the coordinates of 922 Korean festival and event listings against 6,620 registered restaurants using Korea Tourism Organization data. It's structural — and largely predictable in advance.

96 festivals have zero registered restaurants within 3km

Counting registered restaurants within a 3km radius of each festival site: the median is 13. But 96 festivals — 10.4% of the total — have zero. Widening the radius to 10km lifts the median to 63, but 38 festivals still have fewer than 3 restaurants even at that distance.

The regional gap is over 40x

Broken down by province, the median number of restaurants within 3km of a festival site varies enormously:

RegionMedian restaurants within 3km
Seoul85
Incheon / Daejeon27
Busan24
Gyeonggi14
Gangwon / Jeonbuk / Jeonnam / Gyeongbuk4
Chungbuk2

That's a more than 40x gap between Seoul and the lowest-ranked provinces. The instinct that works in Seoul — "we'll just find something nearby" — doesn't transfer to festivals in Gangwon, Chungnam, or Gyeongnam, where "nearby" often means nothing at all.

Famous festivals are often the emptiest

Counterintuitively, some of the best-known festivals have the fewest options nearby, because large festivals need open space and tend to be sited on beaches, riverbanks, or fairgrounds — places that are sparsely populated the rest of the year precisely because they can hold a crowd. Boryeong Mud Festival, which draws hundreds of thousands of visitors annually, has only 4 registered restaurants within 3km of its beach venue. Muju Firefly Festival has 2.

Monday is the most common closing day

Across 6,602 restaurants with registered hours, Monday closures (1,107 restaurants) alone nearly match every other weekday closure combined (1,183 across Tuesday–Saturday). If your festival trip's last day lands on a Monday — common for festivals running through a long weekend — expect your first-choice restaurant to be a coin flip.

Some close earlier than you'd expect

379 restaurants in the dataset close before 3pm — a meaningful number, since festival programming (fireworks, night markets, evening performances) tends to peak later in the day. The well-regarded local spot that shows up in every search result is disproportionately likely to be one that closes early, since these are often places that sell out their prepared ingredients and shut for the day.

Parking usually isn't the problem

Of 6,169 restaurants with parking information listed, 6,143 (99.6%) report having some parking available. The catch: on festival days, restaurant parking lots are frequently absorbed into overflow festival parking, so "the restaurant has parking" doesn't guarantee it'll be available to you specifically.

What to actually do with this

  • Pick your meal before you pick your festival hours, not after — reversing the order usually ends at a convenience store.
  • Outside Seoul/Busan/Incheon, plan on a 10km radius, not 3km.
  • If your last day is a Monday, have a backup restaurant in mind.
  • Eat early, both meals — many places close early, and crowds are thinner before the festival peaks.

Chukjemoa's individual festival pages list nearby restaurants and cafés sorted by distance, along with registered hours and closing days where available — we leave it blank rather than guess when the data isn't there. See What Closes for a broader look at Korean festival and business closing-day patterns before you travel.

title: Where Korean Locals Go vs Where Foreign Visitors Go
desc: Domestic and international visitor data reveal two different maps of Korea. Gangnam is Seoul's #1 destination for Korean travelers — and #6 for foreign ones. Here's what actually explains the gap.
body:
Search for Korea travel recommendations and you'll run into two different lists: the neighborhoods packed with international tourists, and the places Korean travelers and locals actually spend their time. The overlap is smaller than you'd expect.

The nationwide #1 is different for each group

Using Korea Tourism Organization visitor data for a recent 30-day period, the top domestic destination nationwide is Seoul's Gangnam-gu, with 19.19 million domestic visits, followed by Suwon (16.46 million) and Seocho-gu (16.10 million). The top international destination is a different Seoul district entirely — Jung-gu, with 2.55 million foreign visits, followed by Incheon's Jung-gu (1.47 million) and Jeju City (1.32 million).

Gangnam-gu, the domestic #1, ranks only 6th among foreign visitors, at 1.12 million — about a sixth of its domestic visitor count. Seoul's Jung-gu, home to Myeongdong and Namdaemun Market, doesn't crack the domestic top 10 at all. The pattern: international visitor traffic concentrates in central Seoul (Jung-gu, Jongno-gu, Mapo-gu, Yongsan-gu), gateway cities (Incheon), and self-contained destinations like Jeju. Domestic traffic skews toward large population centers that function as everyday commuting and shopping hubs, not just tourist draws.

Busan splits by neighborhood

Busan shows the pattern within a single city. Domestically, Busanjin-gu (5.99 million) narrowly outranks Haeundae-gu (5.74 million) — Busanjin-gu is home to the Seomun shopping and nightlife district, a local favorite. Among foreign visitors, the order flips: Haeundae-gu leads with 749,000, Gangseo-gu (home to Gimhae Airport) is second at 710,000, and Busanjin-gu drops to third at 429,000.

The practical takeaway: if you want Busan's local food-and-shopping scene, Busanjin-gu / Seomun has more of a domestic crowd. If you want the beach-and-skyline image most visitors associate with Busan, Haeundae is the internationally proven choice. Splitting a Busan trip across both is a reasonable way to see both sides.

Gangwon: still mostly a domestic destination

Gangwon province shows the widest gap of all. Domestically, Gangneung is the top destination at 2.96 million visits. Among foreign visitors, Gangneung doesn't even lead its own province — Chuncheon does, with just 69,000 visits — and Gangneung's foreign visitor count (46,000) is only 1.6% of its domestic count. Korea's mountain, valley, and coastal nature destinations tend to be car-dependent and light on multilingual signage, which likely explains a meaningful part of the gap. If quiet, uncrowded nature is what you're after, Gangwon remains relatively undiscovered by international travelers — even though it's currently one of the most crowded provinces for domestic summer travel.

Jeju is the exception

Jeju breaks the pattern entirely — the visitor rankings are nearly identical for both groups. Jeju City ranks #1 for both domestic (4.49 million) and foreign (1.32 million) visitors; Seogwipo ranks #2 for both. Unlike Seoul, Busan, or Incheon, where specific districts pull disproportionate international traffic, Jeju functions as a single, self-contained destination regardless of where a visitor is from.

How to use this

If you want a quieter, more local experience, look for places where the domestic ranking is much higher than the international one — Gangwon's countryside and mid-sized cities are the clearest example. If you'd rather have well-developed multilingual infrastructure, the international top destinations (central Seoul, Haeundae, Jeju) remain a safe, proven choice. Chukjemoa's Rankings page updates this visitor data weekly by region, and you can cross-reference it with what's running in the same area on Festival Finder.

A caveat: this data is a telecom/card-based estimate, not an exact headcount, and international visitor figures may include longer-term residents in addition to short-stay tourists — though the destinations discussed here (central tourist districts, airport-adjacent areas, Jeju) are unlikely to be meaningfully distorted by that. Figures are drawn from a recent 30-day window, so seasonal destinations can rank very differently at other times of year.

title: How to Choose a Mountain to Hike in Korea
desc: The Korea Tourism Organization's English mountain listings span from 30-meter beginner trails to 900-meter peaks, spread across every province. Here's how to pick one that matches your trip.
body:
"Go hiking in Korea" covers an enormous range — from a 30-minute walk on Jeju to a full-day climb in a national park. Korea Tourism Organization's official English-language listings currently cover 65 mountains and hiking areas nationwide, and looking at where they are and how high they go is a useful starting point for picking one that fits your trip.

Where they're concentrated

By province, the 65 listings break down as: Jeju 13, Seoul 9, Gyeongbuk 9, Gangwon 7, Gyeonggi 5, Busan 4, Chungnam 4, Jeonnam 3, Chungbuk 3, Jeonbuk 3, Gyeongnam 2, Ulsan 2, Incheon 1. Jeju's strong showing reflects both its volcanic terrain and its role as a hiking-focused destination in its own right; Seoul's 9 listings are worth noting for travelers without a rental car, since several are reachable directly by subway.

Not every mountain in Korea means a serious climb

Elevation is listed for 32 of the 65 entries (the rest describe the trail or area without stating a summit height). Among those that do, the range is wide. On the low end: Yeongsil Trail inside Hallasan National Park on Jeju sits around 30m of relative elevation gain and is a short, scenic walk rather than a climb; Suwolbong Peak, also on Jeju, is about 77m; Jeombongsan Mountain's Gombaeryeong Pass is around 100m. On the higher end within this list: Daeyasan Mountain reaches about 931m, with Chungnyeongsan (879m), Gubyeongsan (876m), and Gwanggyosan (852m) close behind. In Seoul itself, several listed hills — like Bonghwasan at 160m and Achasan at 295m — are genuinely easy, city-accessible walks with skyline views, not full mountain expeditions.

How to actually pick one

  • Short on time or without a car? Start with Seoul's listed hills (Achasan, Bonghwasan and others) — most are reachable by subway and can be done in half a day.
  • Want a real climb without a multi-day commitment? Look at the entries in the 800–930m range noted above; these need proper footwear and several hours but don't demand technical mountaineering experience.
  • On Jeju already? The island's 13 listings range from short, easy trails near the coast to Hallasan itself — check the specific listing's description, since "mountain" on Jeju covers everything from a 30-minute oreum walk to South Korea's tallest peak.
  • Traveling in autumn? Gyeongbuk and Gangwon's mountain areas are also popular foliage destinations — worth checking When to Go if fall colors are part of the plan.

Browse the full, current list — with location, official description, and photos where available — on Chukjemoa's Mountains page. As with all TourAPI-sourced listings, not every entry includes every detail (elevation, trail length, and difficulty are reported unevenly across sources), so where information isn't listed, it isn't guessed.

title: Bringing Your Dog to a Korean Festival: What to Check First
desc: Pet policies at Korean festivals vary by venue and aren't consistently recorded, even in official data. Here's how to check before you go, and how to keep a dog safe at a summer festival.
body:
If you're traveling with a dog, the first question at any Korean festival is simple: will they actually let us in? The honest answer is that policies vary enormously — sometimes within the same festival, where an outdoor plaza allows pets but an indoor exhibition hall doesn't — and the official data on this is thinner than you'd hope.

An honest look at the data

Looking at the Korea Tourism Organization's national festival database — the 915-festival domestic dataset that underlies Chukjemoa's Korean-language site — only 8 festivals carry an explicit, structured pet-policy flag. That's under 1%. This isn't unique to pet policy; it reflects that Korea's official tourism data generally isn't built to record every practical detail a visitor might want. It also means a missing pet flag says nothing about whether pets are actually allowed — it usually just means the field was never filled in.

Practical takeaway: treat "no information listed" as "confirm directly," not as "probably fine." A phone call to the festival organizer is the only reliable way to know before you travel.

What to actually ask

"Are pets allowed?" isn't specific enough — the useful follow-up questions are: Is it outdoor areas only, or indoor exhibits too? Does the dog need to stay in a carrier, or can it walk on a leash? Is there a size or weight limit? Is there a maximum leash length? Policies can also change year to year, so even a policy you find from a previous year's event is worth reconfirming.

Summer heat is harder on dogs than it looks

A dog at ground level experiences radiant heat from pavement and sand far more intensely than a standing adult does — a simple check is pressing the back of your hand to the ground for five seconds; if it's too hot for your hand, it's too hot for paws. Watch for heavy panting, slowing pace, or reddened gums, and move to shade immediately if you see any of them. Never, under any circumstance, leave a dog alone in a parked car — interior temperatures climb dangerously fast, even briefly.

What to bring

  • Water and a collapsible bowl — drinking water for dogs is often hard to find at festival grounds, and human drinks aren't a substitute.
  • A short leash, around 1.2m — retractable long leads are a hazard in a crowd, both for tangling and for other visitors.
  • ID tag and registration details, confirmed current.
  • Waste bags, more than you think you'll need.
  • A cooling mat or vest, and for small dogs, a carrier or pet stroller — carrying or wheeling through dense crowds is safer than walking at ankle height.

When it's better to leave them home

If daytime highs are above 30°C (86°F), reconsider bringing a dog at all. Water festivals and mud festivals present their own risks — skin irritation and the chance of ingesting something they shouldn't. Large evening fireworks or loud stage performances are genuinely distressing for noise-sensitive dogs, independent of whether pets are technically permitted.

Lower-risk alternatives

An open-air traditional market is generally an easier environment than a festival — open layout, easier to avoid crowds — though it's still worth steering clear of food stalls. A quieter option is browsing what's running near you on Festival Finder and calling ahead before you commit to a specific event with your dog along.
